Information theory is the mathematical study of the quantification, storage, and communication of information. Founded by Claude Shannon in his 1948 paper "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," the discipline treats information not as semantic meaning, but as measurable uncertainty resolved through data transmission.

Core Concepts

  • Information Entropy ($H$): The measure of average uncertainty or surprise in a random variable. The more unpredictable an outcome, the more information it yields when observed: $$H(X) = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} P(x_i) \log_2 P(x_i)$$ Measured in bits (binary digits) when using base-2 logarithms, representing the minimum number of yes/no questions needed on average to determine the outcome.
  • Source Coding (Data Compression): The fundamental limit on how much data can be compressed without losing information (lossless compression) is bounded by the source's entropy. Common implementations include Huffman coding and arithmetic coding.
  • Channel Capacity ($C$): The maximum rate at which information can be transmitted reliably over a noisy communication channel.
  • Shannon-Hartley Theorem: Defines channel capacity for a continuous channel with additive white Gaussian noise: $$C = B \log_2 \left(1 + \frac{S}{N}\right)$$ Where $B$ is bandwidth in Hertz, $S$ is signal power, and $N$ is noise power.
  • Error-Correcting Codes (Channel Coding): Adding structured redundancy to a message so that errors introduced during noisy transmission can be detected and corrected without retransmission (e.g., Hamming codes, Reed-Solomon, LDPC codes).

Primary Applications

  • Telecommunications: Underpins cellular networks (4G/5G), Wi-Fi protocols, and deep-space communications to maximize data throughput near the Shannon limit.
  • Data Storage & Compression: Standard compression algorithms (ZIP, JPEG, MP3) and error-resilient storage on SSDs, hard drives, and optical discs.
  • Cryptography: Provides theoretical definitions of absolute security (such as Shannon's proof of the one-time pad via perfect secrecy).
  • Machine Learning & Statistics: Loss functions like cross-entropy and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measure the statistical divergence between probability distributions.
